title: Agent-mediated labeling: workflows and evaluation

slides.title: The conventional labeling workflow
slides.notes: The conventional workflow places two burdens on the human: making a partly tacit conception explicit as a guideline, and repeatedly applying it to varied items. The warning callouts name possible failure modes, not a claim that every conventional dataset is unreliable. This slide motivates the proposed method rather than reporting a comparative experiment.

slides.title: Use case 1: a human with an idea
slides.notes: The core unit of human work is a consequential judgment about a rule, group, contrast, exception, or conflict. The agent retrieves cases from the corpus and brings a focused question to the human. It records the answer, updates the rule and identifies affected labels. Information and rules evolve with examples rather than being completed before any labeling occurs. The human retains authority over meaning. An accepted output may be a small reviewed subset or a larger batch accepted under a stated audit policy. Unknown or deferred cases remain visible. High-level judgments can coexist with occasional item checks. Both use cases share the same scaling path. After human approval of the standard, test the same guideline across fixed executor models, refine wording without changing approved meaning, qualify an executor, and apply it to the large unlabeled corpus. Audit batches and route uncertain or conflicting cases back for review. The larger labeled corpus is not assumed to have every item manually reviewed. The three visual rows distinguish dialogue, paired accepted outputs, and execution at scale. The dialogue produces both a structured, adaptive guideline and human-approved, guideline-consistent labeled data. This accepted data may be a small reviewed subset. The two outputs remain aligned as human decisions refine the standard. Adaptive means approved meaning can evolve through human review of new evidence; executor-driven wording changes must preserve approved meaning. Both outputs support executor testing; development examples must remain separate from held-out evaluation cases. The model-expanded corpus is accepted under the stated review or audit policy. In the proposed Workbench interface, the dialogue is primarily a sequence of decision reports with rule-level choices and comments. Chat is supplemental. Both channels feed the same versioned decision record.

slides.title: Use case 2: an existing labeled corpus
slides.notes: Existing labels are evidence of prior decisions, not unquestioned ground truth. The agent infers candidate rules and constructs issue groups containing supporting items, conflicting cases, contextual differences, alternative explanations and resolution status. A flag does not establish an error. A reviewer can clarify, correct or defer, and need not be the original annotator. An audit without a reviewer may deliver provisional rules and issue groups without certifying an approved standard. Once meaning is accepted, keep the approved semantics fixed while testing wording across independent executor models. Qualification uses unseen cases before large-scale batches and auditing. This scaling stage also follows use case 1. Uniform performance across all models is a research goal, not an established result. The LEFT labeled corpus is starting evidence, not the target collection. Existing labels may reveal patterns but are not automatically gold labels. The human reviewer confirms, revises or defers candidate rules and issue groups. The RIGHT large unlabeled corpus is a distinct target for expansion and supplies new boundary cases. The shared downstream path is structured guideline, cross-model executor testing, and large-scale labeling with audit. Meaning changes require human approval; wording refinement preserves that meaning. The three visual rows distinguish dialogue, paired accepted outputs, and execution at scale. The dialogue produces both a structured, adaptive guideline and human-approved, guideline-consistent labeled data. This accepted data may be a small reviewed subset. The two outputs remain aligned as human decisions refine the standard. Adaptive means approved meaning can evolve through human review of new evidence; executor-driven wording changes must preserve approved meaning. Both outputs support executor testing; development examples must remain separate from held-out evaluation cases. The model-expanded corpus is accepted under the stated review or audit policy. In the proposed Workbench interface, the dialogue is primarily a sequence of decision reports with rule-level choices and comments. Chat is supplemental. Both channels feed the same versioned decision record.

slides.title: Evaluation 1: human effort and labeling quality
slides.notes: Proposed human study. Compare manual item-level labeling, a human-authored guideline applied by a fixed executor, and agent-mediated guideline formation and labeling. Randomize and counterbalance method order using comparable but separate task sets to reduce carryover. Keep corpus access, task context and downstream executor settings comparable where applicable. Analyze build-from-idea tasks and audit-existing-label tasks separately. Measure total active human time, number and type of judgments, corrections, review effort and subjective workload. Use blinded review of held-out items against task-appropriate adjudicated judgments; for subjective tasks, preserve the intended person's standard and report unresolved disagreement. Select the primary quality metric for the label type before testing. Predefine the acceptable quality difference, and compare effort at comparable quality or under a common budget. In audit tasks, estimate confirmed-issue precision and reviewer effort using independent review. Evaluate natural conflicts separately from deliberately planted label changes. Sampling unflagged cases can help estimate missed issues. Old labels and synthetic perturbations are limited references. Pilot data should guide sample size and power; none is specified yet. No experiment has been run.

slides.title: Evaluation 2: guideline portability and scale
slides.notes: Proposed portability experiment. Hold approved information and rules fixed while comparing initial wording, refinement against a single executor, and refinement against multiple executors. Give refinement methods comparable development data and tuning budgets, and use the same facilitator capability where feasible. Recheck semantic fidelity against the approved standard. Keep development cases, calibration decisions and final evaluation cases separate. Freeze candidate wording and acceptance thresholds before the final test. Test the same guideline in fresh model contexts with fixed weights and allowed inputs only, excluding hidden facilitator conversations. Evaluate inexpensive small, intermediate and strong models, plus previously unseen executor models when feasible. Report quality with uncertainty by model and class, coverage, abstention, cost per accepted item, and human review cost. Select a quality metric suited to the task, such as macro-F1 for appropriate categorical labels, rather than assuming accuracy alone. A useful result raises the weakest required model's quality, limits deterioration of strong models within a predefined tolerance, and lowers total accepted-item cost while meeting coverage requirements. A reduced cross-model gap alone can reflect all models becoming worse. Report guideline-development cost separately and its amortization over corpus volume. If the guideline is revised after test inspection, reserve fresh evaluation cases for the new candidate. Benefits remain hypotheses.

slides.title: An end-to-end agent system
slides.notes:
The Agent system owns orchestration across data preparation, meaning development, expression optimization, executor qualification, production and audit. This is a proposed design, not proof of implementation or results. The human retains semantic authority. Meaning is developed through Steps 2-4, producing a versioned structured rule base, an initial guideline expression and reviewed development labels. Step 5 compiles and improves guideline expression while holding accepted meaning fixed. Executors see guideline and item, not reference labels or hidden facilitator conversation. The evaluator uses approved development labels. Failures classified as semantic or unresolved return to the human with evidence; clear-rule failures may be executor limitations. Freeze and qualification are separate from repeated development. A new semantic version invalidates affected downstream claims. Step 0 transforms the corpus into validated annotation items and reserves held-out groups. Step 1 frames the labeling task using prepared development items and their source metadata.

The Meaning Loop uses Workbench decision reports as the default human interface. Chat remains available and contributes context to the same decision record; a proposed change in meaning still requires explicit human confirmation. Only the Meaning Agent asks the human for semantic decisions. The Expression Agent calls fixed-weight executors, optimizes wording and reports unresolved meaning issues back to the Meaning Agent. The person can respond asynchronously while unrelated exploration and execution of the approved version continue. Forms and model calls are coordinated by the agent system. Workbench integration is the proposed production design; the current local form prototype demonstrates interaction but has no agent-receiving backend.

slides.title: Step 0: transform the corpus into items
slides.notes: Step 0 prepares annotation items from the raw corpus before detailed task framing. The agent proposes an explicit itemization recipe from the source structure and the user's initial request. Human confirms the labeling target and allowed context. The agent implements and checks the transformation. Raw rows are not assumed to equal annotation items: one conversation can yield several target-reply items, each with preceding context. Each item carries stable ID, target, allowed context, source link and leakage group. Keep original annotations separately with provenance; they do not become approved reference labels automatically. Check target boundaries, required context, unique IDs, missing fields and duplicates before partitioning. Keep related targets and near duplicates in one group across splits. Reserve held-out groups before developer browsing; only development items feed Step 1 task framing and the Meaning Loop. New recipe means a new version; preserve raw source. This is a design proposal, not an executed preparation Run.

slides.title: Step 1: frame the labeling task
slides.notes: The Agent elicits purpose, target population, annotation unit and a provisional schema without requiring a complete codebook up front. Use case 1 begins with a vague conception; use case 2 begins with labels that may encode several annotator standards. Human specifies whether to reconstruct a historical standard, assess consistency, or define a new standard suited to the intended use. These are different claims. If no authorized human participates, the system may produce provisional rules and an issue report but should not assert human approval. An uncertain or deferred case is distinct from absence or a negative label. Step 0 has prepared annotation items. Step 1 frames the intended labeling task using those items and source metadata. A changed target or context requirement may require a new item recipe before proceeding. No full guideline is required before Meaning Loop development.

slides.title: Step 2: prepare a decision report
slides.notes: Each round starts from the human's rough idea, source notes, earlier judgments and learning evidence. The agent retrieves typical cases, contrasts, counterexamples and hard cases; random and coverage sampling remain necessary. Group the evidence into consequential decisions rather than one question per item. Each decision report contains questions, traceable source references, current rules, mutually intelligible alternatives, expected changes and the scope of affected items. Difficulty, uncertainty, missing context and rule confusion can themselves be decisions requiring a definition. The agent produces structured report content; Workbench renders a consistent form. Reports can contain a small batch of cards; no fixed batch count is prescribed. Only learning evidence is used to develop guideline content. Both learning and evaluation items may be labeled in separate executor contexts, but evaluation item contents and individual errors do not enter the development report.

slides.title: Step 3: collect preferences in Workbench
slides.notes: Workbench is the intended home for the decision form. Agent-generated questions and source evidence are presented in a consistent interface; the user chooses among alternatives, writes comments, rejects all options with their own proposal, or defers. No option is preselected. Draft saving and submission support asynchronous review, including partial submissions. Submission creates a versioned decision record containing report identity, the base guideline version, selected choice, reasoning, sources and affected scope. Optional chat enters the same decision record as additional context or a proposed decision; casual chat must not silently override approved rules. The agent consumes submitted feedback, reconciles meaning, identifies unresolved issues and prepares the next round. The slide depicts proposed Workbench integration. The working local prototype currently saves drafts in the browser and exports feedback JSON; it does not automatically deliver feedback to an agent or update the guideline.

slides.title: Step 4: integrate feedback and check alignment
slides.notes: Submitted form choices, custom proposals, chat context and earlier decisions enter the Meaning Agent's reconciliation step. Distinguish a genuine change in preference from missing context, a bad summary or inconsistent candidate options. Keep old decisions and their scope instead of silently overwriting them. Apply explicit confirmed meaning, draft clarifications for custom or conflicting submissions, identify affected learning items and recheck counterexamples. The two aligned outputs are a versioned structured adaptive guideline and human-approved reference labels. Rule approval does not automatically make every model-propagated label human-approved; preserve direct review, inferred prediction and audit-based acceptance as distinct provenance states. Unanswered or unresolved issues remain pending and return as focused cards in a later report. Independent work can continue against the approved version. When ready, both approved meaning and the reference subset pass together to the Expression Loop.

slides.title: Step 5: improve expression without changing meaning
slides.notes: Expression Loop. Input is approved meaning, a candidate guideline expression and human-reviewed development labels. Agent rewrites wording, decision order, format and examples while holding accepted rules, conditions, exceptions and priority fixed. It calls independent label executors as tools with fresh contexts and fixed weights. The executor receives the candidate guideline plus item and permitted context, never that item's reference answer. Scoring tools compare predictions with the approved development labels. Agent inspects per-class quality, coverage, weak-model quality, strong-model non-regression, cost and fidelity to meaning. Select candidate expressions under quality constraints; lower inter-model gap alone is insufficient. Approved references can guide development but final qualification remains separate. Pure wording failures stay in the loop. Missing/conflicting rules or suspect reference labels go back to human meaning review with an evidence packet. Clear-rule failures may be executor limitations and do not justify changing the user's standard. Budget exhaustion leads to an explicit unresolved report, not a fabricated success. Training-free means no model parameter updates; prompt/guideline optimization still occurs and can overfit. Performance parity is not guaranteed.

slides.title: Step 6: freeze a version and qualify executors
slides.notes: The agent freezes exact semantic version, expression, output schema and executor settings after development. Before release, define quality and coverage floors, tolerance for strong-model degradation and cost selection policy. Independent human reference judgments should reflect the frozen intended standard and be collected without exposure to executor predictions. Qualification data has not participated in iterative refinement. Score fresh predictions and choose a qualified executor, considering cost including human review. Selecting a model on qualification data is not an unbiased final performance estimate; independent confirmation is needed for the final generalization claim. If failures cause further tuning, those inspected cases are development evidence and require fresh untouched confirmation. Semantic failures return to the human; execution or wording failures return to Step 5. No candidate passing means hold or human-only route. A narrow performance gap is not sufficient.

slides.title: Step 7: label at scale and audit the result
slides.notes: The Agent system executes the end-to-end delivery phase: batches target items, calls qualified executors with the frozen guideline, tracks versions, routes risk cases, reconciles missing or duplicate outputs and conducts audit. Repeat production batches and audits while the frozen standard and acceptance policy hold. Output includes exact guideline version, accepted labels with provenance, unresolved items and quality report. A new meaning defect reopens Steps 2-4 through the human and leads to a new version, affected-label review and requalification. Clear execution failures route to expression or executor selection; never silently overwrite a frozen policy.

slides.title: A decision card inside Workbench
slides.notes: This enlarged decision card is an illustrative form design using synthetic supportiveness examples from the local prototype. It is not real collected user evidence, a prescribed correct labeling rule or an interactive PowerPoint control. The purpose is to show how high-level preferences can be collected through low-friction structured choices. A card presents a clear question, contrastive learning evidence, alternative rules, the current rule, traceable sources, expected effects and affected scope. Users may select an alternative, supply a custom rule, defer, and add comments. All options start unselected. Workbench should render and persist structured agent-generated report content rather than requiring a newly implemented webpage every round. Submission records the person's preference and scope; the Meaning Agent then checks cross-decision consistency and integrates the decision. A rule decision is not automatic item-level approval for propagated labels. Diagnostic decisions can define easy versus hard cases, uncertainty reasons and review actions. Form interaction may be asynchronous; chat supplements the same record.
